newsitem.title: USA: INSIGHT-Oil rally pushes GSCI returns to record.
newsitem.headline: INSIGHT-Oil rally pushes GSCI returns to record.

text.p: Surging oil prices may help boost returns on investments in commodities to fresh record highs in the near future, as measured by the Goldman Sachs Commodity Index's Returns Index, analysts said.

"Growth in worldwide oil consumption is projected to exceed expectations, while increases in non-OPEC supplies are not anticipated to reach forecast levels," said Philip Verleger, analyst with Washington D.C.-based Charles River Associates.

"Distillate markets (heating oil, diesel, gas oil and jet) are expected to remain very, very tight in the Atlantic Basin because of the shift to low-sulfur fuel in Europe and the continued incentive to use diesel there rather than gasoline."
The Goldman Sachs Commodity Index (GSCI) saw a five month high at 214.78 last week, boosting the GSCI Total Returns Index to an all time high at 3392.59 on October 8.

An investment in commodities, weighted according to the GSCI index, produced a return of 42.25 percent in the past 12 months, compared to only 23.43 percent for an investment in U.S. equities weighted according to the S&P500 index.
The GSCI is based on a basket of 22 U.S. and European exchange traded commodities and the returns index is based on an investment in the nearby active month for each commodity.
The indices are used as a benchmark by pension and commodity funds diversifying portfolios into commodities as an asset class.
The gains in the GSCI have been driven by price rises in the energy sector which makes up 49 percent of the index.
NYMEX nearby November crude oil futures were up 32 cents at $24.98 a barrel early Monday, after last week coming close to the five year high of $25.70 seen in April this year.
But "the story of the oil market today is distillate fuel," Verleger said.
NYMEX November heating oil was up 1.57 cents at 73.00 cents a gallon early Monday, after seeing a five year high at 76.75 cents for the nearby contract last week.
U.S. distillate inventories, which usually rise during the lower-demand summer period, failed to rise at all this season.

Meanwhile demand for diesel and heating oil is up 4.6 pct for the first 277 days of 1996 compared to the same period in 1995, driven by U.S. economic growth which ran at an annual rate of 4.8 pct in the second quarter.
But the decline in U.S. distillate stocks is concentrated almost entirely in high-sulfur distillates, used for heating oil, and almost entirely on the East Coast (PADD 1).
East Coast high sulphur fuel oil inventory is 43.9 percent lower than last year at the end of September, according to American Petroleum Institute inventory statistics.

U.S. Gulf Coast refiners currently have a stronger incentive to ship product to Europe than the U.S. Northeast, because of the premium available across the Atlantic and because the U.S. Jones Act mandates domestic supplies must move in U.S.-flagged ships manned by U.S. crews.
But product can be shipped to Europe from the U.S. Gulf in foreign-flagged ships at a lower cost, analysts said.

"The U.S. may need to import distillates this winter, instead of exporting 40,000 bpd, and will be competing with Europe's imports of 100,000 bpd after the EU environmental rule changes," Smith Barney analyst John Saucer said.

European distillate prices have been supported partly by recent European Union regulations mandating a diesel fuel sulfur content reduction to 0.05 percent, a rule similar to the one introduced by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) in October 1993, analysts said.
The regulation means refiners now have to hold separate stocks of high sulphur and low sulphur fuel, rather than stocks of a single product, pushing up costs.

The regulation also prevents Russia and Romania, which produce high sulphur distillates, from supplying Europe. These two countries supply about four percent of EU distillate demand, according to the OECD.

EU distillate fuel consumption has been rising about 1.6 percent a year recently, with the lower tax rate imposed on diesel, compared to gasoline, resulting in over 50 percent of new cars sold in Europe now using diesel.

The consumption shift from gasoline to diesel in Europe has created a gasoline surplus that EU refiners have been exporting, mostly to the U.S., holding down U.S. refiners profit margins on gasoline, Verleger said.
